source.title: SALAD: Systematic Assessment of Machine Unlearning on LLM-Aided Hardware Design
source.authors: Zeng Wang; Ming-Hao Shao; R. Karn; Likhitha Mankali; Jitendra Bhandari; Ramesh Karri; Ozgur Sinanoglu; Muhammad Shafique; J. Knechtel

record.tranche_reason: Tests machine-unlearning effectiveness in a new hardware-design setting using forgetting and utility measures, but does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The study reports unlearning metrics and downstream RTL-generation performance. It does not apply fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery attacks. Values used only to choose unlearning settings are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Applies six standard unlearning methods (GA, GD, PO, NPO, SimNPO, RMU) to fine-tuned LLaMA 3.1-8B in a new domain, hardware/Verilog generation. It reports forget-set leakage (FR, Min-K%++, FP, PrivLeak) and downstream Pass@k. That bears on A's forgetting-plus-utility part only. No recovery attack of any kind is run, so B–F are untested. T3 (new setting) fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude unlearning mitigates contamination, custom-design, IP and malicious-code risks while preserving utility. RMU/SimNPO give the best forgetting–utility trade-off (RMU Pass@15 75 vs 83 clean), and GA/GD erase more aggressively but degrade utility. They do not test recovery attacks.
record.recipe_differences: Implements GA, GD, PO, NPO, SimNPO, and RMU using an OpenUnlearning/TOFU-based framework, but applies them to fine-tuned LLaMA 3.1-8B hardware-design data and evaluates with FR, Min-K%++, and RTL-generation benchmarks rather than testing the claimed recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies across unlearning method, threat dataset, and unlearning epoch; the text reports metric rebounds for some methods and scenarios.
record.peer_reviewed: Workshop on Machine Learning for CAD
record.problems: The forgetting measures (FR and Min-K%++) are not direct demonstrations of chance-level targeted accuracy or recovery resistance. No recovery attacks are tested. The artifact appendix describes the malicious forget data as 1 example and the IP forget data as 2 examples. The paper's prose and flattened figures contain some inconsistent metric descriptions and values.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted additional method-by-epoch results from Figs. 3–7 and many cross-benchmark Pass@K entries to stay within the row limit and prioritize text-described forgetting outcomes and utility. No recovery-attack results are present to extract.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks (relearning, prompting, quantization, ablation) recover the unlearned designs. Also targeted accuracy vs chance (only ROUGE and membership-style scores are used). Utility for the custom, malicious and IP scenarios is not reported in numbers.
No relearning or fine-tuning after unlearning.
No activation ablation or analysis of blocking vs deletion.
No rephrasing, jailbreak or in-context recovery attempts.
No method is evaluated against recovery attacks.

missing.what: Clean vs sensitive vs unlearned comparison per scenario for FP, FR, Min-K, Min-K++ and PrivLeak. Clean-model levels are the right 'forgotten' baseline (e.g., RTLLM clean FR 58.52).
Utility collapse of GA/GD after unlearning (GA fails across all metrics, GD Pass@15 21 on VerilogEval). This is the evidence for the forgetting–utility trade-off.
missing.locator: Table I and Section V-B text

missing.what: PrivLeak and FP trajectories across methods and epochs.

record.verdict_notes: Several values in the prose conflict with the flattened figures (RMU RTLLM FR 44.4 vs 14.4; custom SimNPO/RMU EP labels). Forget-set sizes conflict: 835 and 703 designs in Sec. IV vs 1 and 2 examples in the artifact appendix. Forgetting is measured by ROUGE and membership-inference scores, not chance-level accuracy. The record's single all-rows limits_scope label is replaced by condition-specific labels. The second label's row_ids key typo should be read as row_ids.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures forgetting and downstream utility, but does not test whether simple attacks recover the targeted knowledge or directly measure targeted accuracy against chance.
No relearning or recovery fine-tuning after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation or test of access-blocking versus deletion.
No method is tested for resisting the recovery attacks listed in the claim.

Table III clean references (FR/Min-K%++): RTLLM 58.52/46.31, VerilogEval 70.24/53.69, custom 37.01/60.58, IP 37.85/74.56, malicious 74.33/38.42. Most RMU/SimNPO values sit at or below these, while GA/GD near-zero values are over-forgetting. Sec IV lists 835 malicious and 703 IP designs, but the artifact appendix gives forget sets of 1 and 2 examples. Pass@k is reported only for benchmark contamination. No attacks.

statements.correction: SALAD (arXiv:2506.02089): LLaMA 3.1-8B fine-tuned on RTL data; the malicious-code forget set is 1 example (artifact appendix). GA FR 94.3 to 2.8 at EP1 on malicious code; no utility number for this scenario. Sec IX: GA/GD harm downstream Verilog generation. On RTLLM-contaminated models, GA VerilogEval Pass@15 is 1 and GD 21 at EP3 (clean 83). RMU malicious FR 8.5 and Min-K%++ 2.6 at EP3, utility unreported. No recovery attacks.
statements.problem: The block cites SALAD's r11 but never names the study or gives any of its numbers. r11 is a GA forgetting-only row, and the study says GA/GD harm downstream Verilog generation, so as support for A it needs that caveat.
